questions.q: Which statement best describes RMSE compared with MAE?
options: RMSE is always smaller than MAE
RMSE squares errors before averaging, so large misses count for more than in MAE
RMSE ignores the sign of the error but MAE does not
RMSE can only be used on percentage data
questions.explain: Squaring makes big errors dominate. RMSE is never smaller than MAE on the same errors, and it is preferred when large misses are especially costly.

questions.q: Why is MAPE risky for a series that sometimes gets close to zero?
options: It divides each error by the actual value, so tiny actuals produce huge or undefined percentages
It cannot handle negative forecasts
It ignores the size of the error entirely
It only works for daily data
questions.explain: MAPE divides by the actual value. Near zero, the percentage explodes, and at exactly zero it is undefined. MASE or MAE are safer choices there.

questions.q: A forecast has a MASE of 0.87, where the scale is the in-sample error of a seasonal naive forecast. What does that tell you?
options: The forecast is 87% accurate
The forecast is worse than the naive baseline
On average the forecast error is smaller than the naive method's in-sample one-step error
The forecast is biased upward by 13%
questions.explain: MASE is a ratio to a naive benchmark's error. Below 1 means the forecast error is smaller than the benchmark's, above 1 means larger. It is not an accuracy percentage.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, the model won on one 28-day holdout but lost on average across five rolling-origin windows. What is the takeaway?
options: Rolling-origin backtesting is unreliable and should be avoided
Seasonal naive is always the best model
The metrics were computed incorrectly on the single split
A single train/test split can give a misleading verdict, so evaluate across several origins and look at the variation
questions.explain: Different windows can favor different models. Backtesting across several origins gives a more honest estimate of future performance and shows how stable it is.

questions.q: What is the correct procedure for a rolling-origin backtest?
options: Shuffle the rows, then run K-fold cross-validation
Train once on all data and score on the same data
Pick an origin date, train only on data before it, forecast the next window, then move the origin forward and repeat
Train on the most recent window and test on the oldest one
questions.explain: Each step trains only on the past and forecasts forward, mimicking production. Repeating it across origins gives several out-of-sample scores.
